title: [Chapitre] I. Vers une géométrie des formes (topologiques) : notes manuscrites (05/06/1986).

deep.reconstruction:
This page sits in a June 1986 attempt to axiomatize one-dimensional 'shapes' (formes topologiques) without point-set topology.

The primitive data, from the preceding pages, are:
- a set L of 'lieux' (places);
- a family S ⊂ 𝔓(L) of 'segments';
- for each segment I, a 'boundary' ∂I ∈ 𝔓₂(I), a two-element subset of endpoints. The interior is I° = I ∖ ∂I.

These data are subject to axioms F1–F6. Among them are:
- a gluing ('recollement') axiom: two segments meeting only in a common endpoint, with different branches there, glue uniquely to a segment;
- sub-segments I_{x,y};
- F6, a filtering condition: segments ending at x and defining the same 'branch' at x are dominated by a common segment.

On this page (dated 7 June) Grothendieck fixes terminology.
- A model of such a '1-form' is called a **réseau** (network).
- The critical or singular places (the set L_s) are the **nœuds** (nodes); the word 'branchement' is crossed out and replaced by 'singuliers'.
- The connected components of the regular part L_r = L ∖ L_s are the **lignes**, preferably called **arêtes** (edges).
- The connected components of the whole structure are the components of the network.
- Each node, and more generally each place, has an **order or multiplicity**: in effect the number of branches (valence) there. It equals 2 at a regular place.

Two extreme classes are then defined.
- **Divisible**: every segment has nonempty interior, so segments can always be subdivided. This is the continuum-like case, as in the geometric realization of a graph.
- **Reduced**: every segment has empty interior, i.e. I = ∂I, card I = 2. Equivalently L_r = ∅: every place is a node.

The next page confirms the purpose. A reduced ('discrete') network on L is just a subset S ⊂ 𝔓₂(L), since the axioms become vacuous there, i.e. a simple graph. Grothendieck then turns to studying connected, nonempty regular networks via case analysis of two 'converging' segments.

The point of the framework is a single axiomatic language in which combinatorial graphs (reduced) and topological graphs / 1-dimensional polyhedra (divisible) are two faces of one notion. Nodes and edges are recovered intrinsically from the segment structure.
errors: No mathematical errors on this page; it consists of definitions.
Minor ambiguity: 'comp. connexes de L_r ∖ L_s' is redundant if L_r is already the complement of L_s. The intended set is presumably L ∖ L_s = L_r.

'Multiplicity of a place' is not defined precisely here. Presumably it is the number of branches at x as defined via F6 on the previous page. That is consistent with the value 2 at regular places, but the infinite-branching case is not addressed.

ideas.what: Axiomatic notion of a 1-dimensional 'network' via places, segments and two-point boundaries satisfying gluing and branching axioms
ideas.modern_name: Synthetic/axiomatic theory of graphs and 1-dimensional continua; close to betweenness or interval structures, axiomatic characterizations of arcs and graphs (Moore-type), and 'segment systems'
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical continuum theory (R.L. Moore, Whyburn) for topological characterizations; various authors for betweenness/interval axiomatics
ideas.where_published: Only the general wish for a 'tame' topology of shapes appears in Esquisse d'un programme (§5); this axiomatics does not, to my knowledge.

ideas.what: Nodes = singular places, edges = connected components of the regular locus, multiplicity = number of branches (2 at regular points)
ideas.modern_name: Vertices of valence ≠ 2 and edges of a topological graph; valence/order of a point in a graph (Menger–Urysohn order)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Standard (Menger–Urysohn order of a point; topological graph theory)

ideas.what: Divisible vs reduced networks: segments always subdivisible versus every segment equal to its two endpoints; a reduced network is the same as a simple graph
ideas.modern_name: Geometric realization / subdivision versus combinatorial graph; dense-order versus discrete case

missed.claim: An intrinsic, point-set-free axiomatics of 1-dimensional shapes (axioms F1–F6) that treats discrete graphs and continuous networks uniformly. Combinatorial graphs appear as the 'reduced' models, and 'divisible' models are continuum-like. The program (classifying connected regular networks, then presumably higher-dimensional 'formes') is begun but not completed in the record.
missed.quote: Un[e] modèle de 1-forme au sens précédent ... satisfaisant les conditions (F1) à (F6)) est appelé un réseau. ... On dira qu'il est réduit si pour tout segment I, I° = ∅ ... i.e. tous ses lieux sont des noeuds.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It is a concrete early step of Grothendieck's 'tame topology / géométrie des formes' program. That program is known mostly from the Esquisse, and this axiomatics is not developed in the literature. It could be compared with o-minimal 1-dimensional definable sets, with R-trees and metric graphs, and with tropical/metric-graph foundations. However, the content on this page itself is definitional.

deep.surprise_reason: The page only fixes vocabulary (network, node, edge, multiplicity, divisible, reduced) for an unpublished axiomatic framework. The framework is a little-known Grothendieck project, but the definitions themselves are natural and standard in spirit.
transcription_corrections: Line 1 likely reads 'Une notion/modèle de 1-forme' (the 'e' of 'Une' is visible).
'[-...-] des faisceaux[?] : satisfaisant les conditions' should most likely read 'de façon à satisfaire les conditions (F1) à (F6))'. There are no sheaves here.
'Les comp. connexes de L_r ∖ L_s' is probably intended as 'L ∖ L_s'; the word 'noeuds' is written beneath L_s as a gloss.
'divisible si[?] pour tout segment' may read 'divisible strict pour tout segment' or 'si et seulement si'; the reading is uncertain.
'est égale à 2 en un lieu régulier' is correct; this is the multiplicity at regular places.
